beats.script_body: A locked, unmarked door on the 102nd-floor observation deck leads to one of New York's most outrageous pie-in-the-sky projects: a narrow terrace intended to dock zeppelins. Spearheading the dream was former New York governor Alfred E Smith, who went from failed presidential candidate in 1928 to head honcho of the Empire State Building project. When architect William Van Alen revealed the secret spire of his competing Chrysler Building, Smith went one better, declaring the Empire State Building would sport an even taller mooring mast for transatlantic airships. The plan had two major oversights: dirigibles require anchoring at both ends, not just at the nose, and passengers cannot exit the craft through the giant helium-filled balloon. That didn't stop them trying. In September 1931 the New York Evening Journal moored a zeppelin and delivered a pile of newspapers fresh out of Lower Manhattan. The docking plan never got off the ground, but years later an aircraft met the building with tragic consequences: a B-25 bomber crashed into the 79th floor on a foggy day in 1945, killing 14 people.

beats.source_passage: A locked, unmarked door on the 102nd-floor observation deck leads to one of New York's most outrageous pie-in-the-sky projects to date: a narrow terrace intended to dock zeppelins. Spearheading the dream was former New York governor Alfred E Smith, who went from failed presidential candidate in 1928 to head honcho of the Empire State Building project. When architect William Van Alen revealed the secret spire of his competing Chrysler Building, Smith went one better, declaring that the top of the Empire State Building would sport an even taller mooring mast for transatlantic airships. While the plan looked good on paper, there were two (major) oversights: dirigibles require anchoring at both ends (not just at the nose, as planned) and passengers (who travel in the zeppelin's gondola) cannot exit the craft through the giant helium-filled balloon. Regardless, it didn't stop them from trying. In September 1931, the New York Evening Journal threw sanity to the wind, managing to moor a zeppelin and deliver a pile of newspapers fresh out of Lower Manhattan. Though the ambitious plan for docking airships never got off the ground, years later an aircraft met up with the building with tragic consequences: a B-25 bomber crashed into the 79th floor on a foggy day in 1945, killing 14 people.

beats.script_body: At the turn of the 20th century, Times Square was an unremarkable intersection known as Longacre Sq. That changed through a deal between subway pioneer August Belmont and New York Times publisher Adolph Ochs. Heading construction of the city's first subway line — from Lower Manhattan to Harlem — Belmont astutely realized that a Midtown business hub would encourage use of the line and maximize profit. He approached Ochs, arguing that moving to Broadway and 42nd St would be a win-win for the broadsheet: an in-house subway station would mean faster distribution of the newspaper, but also more sales to the influx of commuters. Belmont convinced mayor George B McClellan Jr to rename the square in honor of the broadsheet. In the winter of 1904–05, both the subway station and the Times' new headquarters at One Times Square made their debut.

beats.script_body: The neighborhood's first playhouse was the long-gone Empire, opened in 1893 on Broadway between 40th and 41st Sts. Two years later, cigar manufacturer and part-time comedy scribe Oscar Hammerstein opened the Olympia, before opening the Republic — now children's theater New Victory — in 1900. That led to a string of new venues, including the still-beating New Amsterdam Theatre and the Lyceum Theatre. The Broadway of the 1920s was known for lighthearted musicals fusing vaudeville and music-hall traditions, producing classic tunes like Cole Porter's 'Let's Misbehave.' But Midtown's theater district was also evolving as a platform for new American dramatists. One of the greatest was Eugene O'Neill, born in Times Square at the long-gone Barrett Hotel at 1500 Broadway. The playwright debuted many of his works here, including Pulitzer Prize winners Beyond the Horizon and Anna Christie. His success paved the way for other 20th-century greats — Tennessee Williams, Arthur Miller and Edward Albee — recognized by the establishment of the annual Tony Awards in 1947.
